Cells
● Cells: the basic structural and functional units of
  every organism
  ○ All cells:
     1. Are bound by a plasma membrane
     2. Contain cytosol
     3. Contain chromosomes
     4. Contain ribosomes

Cells
There are two types of cells: prokaryotes and
eukaryotes
     Prokaryotes                   Eukaryotes
● Domains Bacteria and       ● Protists, fungi,
  Archaea                      animals, and plants
● DNA is in the nucleoid     ● DNA is in the nucleus
  region                     ● Contain membrane
● Generally smaller in         bound organelles
  size than eukaryotes
Organelles

Organelles
Organelles: membrane bound structures in eukaryotes
Two classifications:
Endomembrane organelles
  1. Nuclear envelope
  2. Endoplasmic reticulum
  3. Golgi complex
  4. Lysosomes
  5. Vesicles/Vacuoles
  6. Plasma membrane
Energy organelles
  1. Mitochondria
  2. Chloroplasts

Compartmentalization
● Compartmentalization in organelles allows for
  different metabolic reactions to occur in different
  locations
   ○ Increases surface area for reactions to occur
   ○ Prevents interfering reactions from occuring in
      the same location




                                              Topic 2.10

Unique Cell Components
         Plants            Animals
● Chloroplasts      ● Lysosomes
● Central vacuole   ● Centrosomes
● Cell wall         ● Flagella
● Plasmodesmata

Endomembrane
  Organelles

Nucleus
● Contains chromosomes (genetic
  information)
   ○ Enclosed by the nuclear
     envelope
      ■ Double membrane
   ○ Has pores
      ■ Pores regulate entry and
        exit of materials from the
        cell

Nucleus
Contains a nucleolus
 ● Dense region of the nucleus
   where ribosomal RNA (rRNA) is
   synthesized
   ○ rRNA is combined with proteins
      to form large and small
      subunits of ribosomes
   ○ Subunits exit via nuclear pores
        ■ Assemble into ribosomes
          ● Ribosomes translate messages found on
             mRNA into the primary structure of
             polypeptides

Review
In order for DNA to leave the nucleus, it must first be
transcribed by RNA polymerase into messenger
RNA (mRNA). The mRNA transcript must then be
modified before leaving the nucleus to the
cytoplasm. In the cytoplasm, the ribosomes decode
the information in mRNA and form continuous
chains of amino acids, thus forming a protein. This
process of DNA → RNA → protein is known as
transcription and translation and will be the main
concepts covered in Unit 6. Answer questions 1-3.

Ribosomes
● Comprised of ribosomal RNA and protein
  ○ Function: synthesize proteins

      Note: some texts do not classify
      ribosomes as organelles because they
      are not bound by a membrane

Ribosomes
● Can be found in two locations:
   1. Cytosol
       ○ Proteins produced here generally
         function only within the cytosol
         (i.e. enzymes)
       ○ Known as “free ribosomes”
   2. Bound to the endoplasmic reticulum
      or nuclear envelope
       ○ Proteins produced here can be
         secreted from the cell
           ■ Leave via transport vesicles

Endoplasmic Reticulum
● A network of membranous sacs and tubes
  ○ Functions:
     ■ Synthesizes membranes
     ■ Compartmentalize the cell to keep proteins
        formed in the rough ER separate from those of
        free ribosomes

Endoplasmic Reticulum
● Two types: rough and smooth

Endoplasmic Reticulum
1. Rough ER
  ○   Contains ribosomes bound to the ER membrane




2. Smooth ER
 ● Contains no ribosomes
 ● Synthesizes lipids,
   metabolizes carbohydrates,
   and detoxifies the cell

Golgi Complex
Contains flattened membranous sacs called
cisternae
  ● Separate the sacs from the cytosol
  ● Each cisternae is not connected
  ● Has directionality
     ○ Cis face:
        ■ Receives vesicles from the ER
     ○ Trans face:
        ■ Sends vesicles back out into cytosol to other
           locations or to the plasma membrane for
           secretion

Golgi Complex
Functions:
● Receives transport vesicles with materials
  from the ER
                             Ensures newly
● Modifies the materials     formed proteins are
● Sorts the materials        folded correctly or
● Adds molecular tags        modified correctly

● Packages materials into new transport
  vesicles that exit the membrane via
  exocytosis

Lysosomes
Membranous sac with hydrolytic enzymes
 ● Function:
   ○ Hydrolyzes macromolecules in animal cells
   ○ Autophagy: lysosomes can recycle their own cell’s
     organic materials
      ■ Allows the cell to renew itself
Peroxisomes
● Similar to lysosomes
● Membrane bound metabolic
  compartment
   ○ Catalyze reactions that produce H2O2
     ■ Enzymes in peroxisomes then
        break down H2O2 to water

Vacuoles
Large vesicles that stem from the ER and Golgi
● Selective in transport
Types:
Food vacuole
● Form via phagocytosis (cell eating) and then are
   digested by lysosomes
Contractile vacuole
● Maintain water levels in cells
Central vacuole
● Found in plants
   ○ Contains inorganic ions and water
   ○ Important for turgor pressure

Practice FRQ
1. Hepatitis C is a virus that attacks the liver and can
   cause liver disease. Liver disease has been linked to
   a reduction in albumin levels in patients analyzed.
   Albumin is an important protein in humans. It
   functions primarily to regulate oncotic pressure of
   blood, which is important for the regulation of fluids in
   vessels of the body and tissue repair. On average,
   patients with liver disease show a 10-30% decrease
   in blood-albumin levels. (a) Identify the organelle in
   liver cells that is most likely being affected by
   hepatitis C and (b) justify your reasoning.

Practice FRQ
2. In humans, pancreatic cells synthesize the protein
  insulin in the endoplasmic reticulum (ER).
  Patients diagnosed with type 1 diabetes have
  immune systems that mistakenly attack their
  pancreatic cells. Therefore, these patients cannot
  produce the hormone insulin and have to take
  medications to introduce insulin into their bodies.
  (a) Describe how insulin would be produced in a
  normal functioning (non-type 1 diabetes)
  pancreatic cell.
Energy Organelles

Endosymbiont Theory
● Endosymbiont Theory: the theory that explains
  the similarities mitochondria and chloroplasts have
  to a prokaryote
   ○ Theory states that an early eukaryotic cell
     engulfed a prokaryotic cell
      ■ Prokaryotic cell became an endosymbiont
        (cell that lives in another cell)
         ● Became one functional organism




                                                Topic 2.11

Endosymbiont Theory
● Evidence:
  ● Double membrane
  ● Ribosomes
  ● Circular DNA
  ● Capable of functioning on their own




                                          Topic 2.11

Mitochondria
Site of cellular respiration
● Structure of the double membrane:
   ○ Outer membrane is smooth
   ○ Inner membrane has folds called cristae
       ■ Divides the mitochondria into two internal
         compartments and increases the surface
         area

Mitochondria
1. Intermembrane: space between inner and
   outer membrane
2. Mitochondrial matrix: enclosed by inner
   membrane
         ● Location for the Krebs cycle
         ● Contains:
           ○ Enzymes that catalyze cellular
              respiration and produce ATP
           ○ Mitochondrial DNA
           ○ Ribosomes

Mitochondria
The number of mitochondria in a cell correlates with
metabolic activity
● Cells with high metabolic activity have more
  mitochondria
   ○ Example: cells that move/contract

Chloroplast
● Specialized organelles in
  photosynthetic organisms
   ○ Site of photosynthesis
   ○ Contains the green pigment
     chlorophyll
● Inside of its double membrane:
   ○ Thylakoids
      ■ Membranous sacs that can
        organize into stacks called
        grana
         ● Light dependent reactions
            occur in grana

Chloroplast
● Stroma: fluid around thylakoids
  ○ Location for the Calvin cycle
  ○ Contains
     ■ Chloroplast DNA
     ■ Ribosomes
     ■ Enzymes
The Cytoskeleton

Cytoskeleton
● A network of fibers throughout the cytoplasm
  ○ Give structural support (especially for animal
     cells) and mechanical support:
     ■ Anchor organelles
     ■ Allow for movement of vesicles and
        organelles and/or the whole cell
         ● Movement occurs when the cytoskeleton
            interacts with motor proteins

Cytoskeleton
There are 3 types of fibers in the cytoskeleton:
   1. Microtubules
   2. Microfilaments
   3. Intermediate filaments

Microtubules
Hollow rod-like structures made of the protein tubulin
● Grow from the centrosome
   ○ Assist in microtubule assembly

Microtubules
Functions:
● Serve as structural support (think: tracks) for the
  movement of organelles that are interacting with
  motor proteins
● Assist in the separation of chromosomes during cell
  division
● Cell motility (i.e., cilia and flagella)

Microfilaments
Thin solid rods made of the protein actin
Functions:
● Maintain cell shape
   ○ Bear tension
● Assist in muscle contraction and cell motility
   ○ Actin works with another protein called myosin
      to cause a contraction
● Division of animal cells
   ○ Contractile ring of the cleavage furrow

Intermediate Filaments
● Fibrous proteins made up of varying subunits
● Permanent structural elements of cells
Functions:
● Maintain cell shape
● Anchor nucleus and organelles
● Form the nuclear lamina
   ○ Lines the nuclear envelope

Practice FRQ
1. You are working in a research lab and your goal is to determine the
   effect that alcohol has on the liver. You design an experiment where you
   expose samples of liver tissues to varying concentrations of alcohol as
   follows:
              Sample         Concentration of alcohol    Duration of exposure

       Sample 1              0.25 mg/mL                 20 minutes

       Sample 2              0.35 mg/mL                 20 minutes

       Sample 3              0.45 mg/mL                 20 minutes

After exposure to the alcohol, you analyze the liver samples. In all samples
you find that the alcohol has been broken down (detoxified). However, in
sample 3 you find damage to organelles has occured due to the high
concentration of alcohol. (a) Identify one organelle in the liver that could be
responsible for the detoxification of the alcohol in all three samples. (b) In
sample 3 identify the organelle that would most likely be responsible for
removing the damaged parts of organelles and (c) describe the steps it
would take to do so.

Cell Size
Cellular metabolism depends on cell size


                          Cellular waste must leave
                          Dissipate thermal energy
                          Nutrients and other
                          resources/chemical materials
                          must enter

At a certain size, it begins to be too difficult for a cell
to regulate what comes in and what goes out of the
plasma membrane

Surface Area and Volume
The size of a cell will dictate the function
● Cells need a high surface area-to-volume ratio to
  optimize the exchange of material through the
  plasma membrane

Formulas
● Formulas for cuboidal cells
  ○ Total SA= height x width x number of sides x
    number of boxes (or SA = 6S2 if only 1 box)
  ○ Total V= height x width x length x number of
    boxes (or V = S3 if only one box)
  ○ SA to V ratio = SA/V
● Formulas for spherical cells
  ○ SA = 4πr2
                                 Remember: all
  ○ V = 4/3πr3                   formulas are given
  ○ SA:V ratio = SA/V            to you on the AP
                                 exam

What Does This Mean for a Cell?
Cells tend to be small
● Small cells have a high SA:V ratio
   ○ Optimizes exchange of materials at the plasma
      membrane
● Larger cells have a lower SA:V ratio
   ○ Lose efficiency exchanging materials
       ■ The cellular demand for resources
         increases
       ■ Rate of heat exchange decreases

Plasma Membrane
Answer review questions 2-4

Plasma Membrane
Separates internal cell
environment from external
environment
● Comprised primarily of
  phospholipids
● Phospholipids are amphipathic
   ○ Hydrophilic head and
     hydrophobic tails
   ○ Forms a bilayer

Plasma Membrane
Selective permeability: The ability
of membranes to regulate the
substances that enter and exit
 Hydrophilic heads oriented
 TOWARD aqueous
 environments
 Hydrophobic tails are facing
 inwards AWAY from
 aqueous environments

Fluid Mosaic Model
A model to describe the structure of
cell membranes
● Fluid: membrane is held
   together by weak hydrophobic
   interactions and can therefore
   move and shift
    ○ Temperature affects fluidity
    ○ Unsaturated hydrocarbon
       tails help maintain fluidity at
       low temps
        ■ Kinked tails prevent tight
           packing of phospholipids

Fluid Mosaic Model
  ○ Cholesterol helps maintain
    fluidity at high and low
    temps
     ■ High temp: reduces
        movement
     ■ Low temp: reduces tight
        packing of
        phospholipids
● Mosaic: comprised of many
  macromolecules

Membrane Proteins
There are two major
categories of proteins in the
membrane
1. Integral proteins
    ○ Proteins that are
       embedded into the lipid
       bilayer
       ■ aka transmembrane
           proteins
       ■ Amphipathic
 2. Peripheral proteins
     ○ Proteins that are not embedded into the lipid bilayer
        ■ Loosely bonded to the surface

Membrane Carbohydrates
Important for cell-to-cell recognition
 ● Glycolipids
   ○ Carbohydrates bonded to lipids
● Glycoproteins
   ○ Carbohydrates bonded to proteins
   ○ Most abundant
Plant Cells

Plants
Plants have a cell wall that cover their plasma
membranes
● Extracellular structure (not found in animal cells)
   ○ Provides:
      ■ Shape/structure
      ■ Protection
      ■ Regulation of water intake

Plants
● The cell wall is composed of
  cellulose
● Thicker than plasma membranes
● Contain plasmodesmata
  ○ Hole-like structures in the cell
     wall filled with cytosol that
     connect adjacent cells

Practice FRQ
The Channichthyidae fish, also known as the crocodile
ice fish, lives in the Southern Ocean around Antarctica.
These waters are known to maintain extremely low
temperatures all year, ranging from approximately 28℉
to 35℉. These fish have adaptations that allow them to
live in cold, low oxygen waters. (a) Describe the
expected membrane lipid composition of the cells from
the Channichthyidae fish. (b) Explain how the
membrane lipid composition you described in part (a)
is advantageous for the fish's survival in its
environment.

Work on the practice problems.

Selective Permeability
Some substances can cross the membrane more
easily than others
Easy passage across the membrane:
● Small nonpolar, hydrophobic molecules
     ○ Examples:
        ■ Hydrocarbons
        ■ CO2, O2, N2
Difficult passage or protein assisted passage:
● Hydrophilic, polar molecules, large molecules, ions
     ○ Examples:
        ■ Sugars, water

Transport Across a Membrane
There are two main types of transport across a
membrane: passive and active

Passive Transport
● Passive transport: transport of a molecule that
  does not require energy from the cell because a
  solute is moving with its concentration or
  electrochemical gradient
  ○ Involved in the import of materials and export
     of waste
  ○ Examples:
     ■ Diffusion
     ■ Osmosis
     ■ Facilitated diffusion

Passive Transport
● Diffusion: spontaneous process resulting from
  the constant motion of molecules
   ○ Substances move from a high to low
     concentration
     ■ Move DOWN the concentration gradient

Passive Transport
Molecules diffuse directly across membrane
● Different rates of diffusion for different molecules



                                          Remember:
                                          even with
                                          diffusion the
                                          membrane is
                                          still selectively
                                          permeable

Passive Transport
Osmosis: the diffusion of water down its concentration
gradient across a selectively permeable membrane
● Can also be thought of as the diffusion of water
   from areas of low solute concentration to areas of
   high solute concentration

Passive Transport
● Facilitated diffusion: diffusion of molecules
  through the membrane via transport proteins
   ○ Increases rate of diffusion for:
      ■ Small ions, water, carbohydrates
   ○ Two categories of transport proteins: channel
     and carrier
      ■ Each transport protein is specific for
         substances it can facilitate movement for

Passive Transport
● Why is facilitated diffusion passive transport and
  not active transport?
  ○ Facilitated diffusion is still passive transport
     because the substances the proteins are
     helping to move are moving DOWN their
     concentration gradient and NO energy is
     required

Passive Transport
● Channel proteins: provide a channel for molecules and
  ions to pass
   ○ Channel is hydrophilic
         ● Many are gated channels
            ○ Only allow passage when there is a
               stimulus
         ● Aquaporins: specific channel protein for water

Passive Transport
Carrier proteins: undergo conformational changes
for substances to pass

Active Transport
● Active transport: transport of a molecule that
  requires energy because it moves a solute
  against its concentration gradient
     ■ Pumps
     ■ Cotransport
     ■ Exocytosis
     ■ Endocytosis

Active Transport
● Active transport requires energy
  ○ Adenosine Triphosphate (ATP): Energy source
    used by cells
    ○ ATP can transfer the terminal phosphate group to
       the transport protein, which changes the shape
       of the transport protein to better move a
       substance

                                        Also known as
                                        conformational
                                        change

Active Transport
Pumps: maintain membrane potential
● Membrane potential: unequal concentrations of
  ions across the membrane results in an electrical
  charge (electrochemical gradient)
   ○ The cytoplasm is relatively negative in
     comparison to the extracellular fluid
   ○ Energy is stored in electrochemical gradients

Active Transport
Examples of pumps:
Electrogenic pumps: proteins that generate voltage
across membranes, which can be used later as an
energy source for cellular processes
● Sodium potassium pump
  ○ Animal cells will regulate their relative concentrations
     of Na+ and K+
     ■ 3 Na+ get pumped out of the cell
     ■ 2 K+ get pumped into the cell
         ● Results in a +1 net charge to the extracellular
           fluid

Active Transport
Examples of pumps:
● Proton pump: integral membrane protein that builds
  up a proton gradient across the membrane
   ○ Used by plants, fungi, and bacteria
   ○ Pumps H+ out of the cell

Active Transport
● Cotransport: the coupling of a favorable
  movement of one substance with an unfavorable
  movement of another substance
  ○ Uses the energy stored in electrochemical
    gradients (generated by pumps) to move
    substances against their concentration
    gradient

Active Transport
● Favorable movement: downhill diffusion
● Unfavorable movement: uphill transport

Active Transport
● Plants use cotransport for sugars and amino acids
● Example: sucrose-H+ cotransporter
  ○ Sucrose can travel into a plant cell against its
     concentration gradient ONLY if it is coupled with
     H+ that is diffusing down its electrochemical
     gradient
Cotransport

Active Transport
Transport of large molecules is done through
exocytosis and endocytosis
Exocytosis: the secretion of molecules via vesicles
that fuse to the plasma membrane
 ● Vesicles can fuse to the membrane by forming a
   bilayer
      ○ Once fused, the contents of the vesicle are
        released to the extracellular fluid
      ○ Example: nerve cells releasing
        neurotransmitters

Active Transport
Endocytosis: the uptake of molecules from vesicles
fused from the plasma membrane (think: opposite of
exocytosis)
 ● Phagocytosis
 ● Pinocytosis
 ● Receptor-mediated

Active Transport
Phagocytosis: when a cell engulfs particles to be
later digested by lysosomes

● Cell surrounds particle
  with pseudopodia
● Packages particles
  into a food vacuole
   ○ Food vacuole fuses
     with a lysosome to
     be digested

Active Transport
Pinocytosis: nonspecific uptake of extracellular fluid
containing dissolved molecules

● Cell takes in
  dissolved molecules
  in a protein coated
  vesicle
   ○ Protein coat helps
     to mediate the
     transport of
     molecules

Active Transport
Receptor mediated endocytosis: specific uptake of
molecules via solute binding to receptors on the
plasma membrane

● Allows the cell to take
  up large quantities of a
  specific substance
● When solutes bind to
  the receptors, they
  cluster in a coated
  vesicle to be taken into
  the cell

Water Balance
Tonicity: the ability of an extracellular solution to cause a
cell to gain or lose water
 ● Depends on the concentration of solutes that cannot
     pass through the cell membrane
 ● Cells can be in three types of solutions:
        ○ Isotonic
        ○ Hypertonic
        ○ Hypotonic
 ● Osmoregulation: cells must be able to regulate their
     solute concentrations and maintain water balance
        ○ Animal cells will react differently than cells with
           cell walls, like plants, fungi, and some protists

Tonicity: Isotonic Solutions
Cells immersed in an isotonic solution have no net
movement of water
● The concentration of nonpenetrating solutes inside the
  cell is equal to that outside the cell.
    ○ Water diffuses into the cell at the same rate water
       moves out of the cell                Plant Cell
          Animal Cell

Tonicity: Hypertonic Solutions
Cells immersed in a hypertonic solution lose water to their
extracellular surroundings
● The concentration of nonpenetrating solutes is higher
   outside of the cell
    ○ Water will move to the extracellular fluid
       ■ Cells shrivel and die                 Plant Cell


      Animal Cell     Plasmolysis:
                      vacuole shrinks
                      and the plasma
                      membrane pulls
                      away from the
                      cell wall

Tonicity: Hypotonic Solutions
Cells immersed in a hypotonic solution gain water
● The concentration of nonpenetrating solutes is lower
  outside of the cell
    ○ The cell will gain water
       ■ Animal cells swell and lyse        Plant Cell
       ■ Plant cells work optimally

      Animal Cell

                          Maintain
                          turgor
                          pressure

Water Potential
Water potential: a physical property that predicts the
direction water will flow
● Includes the effects of solute concentration and
   physical pressure
      ○ Water will flow from areas of:
         ■ High water potential to areas of low water
           potential
         ■ Low solute to areas of high solute
           concentration
         ■ High pressure to areas of low pressure

ced_current_atoms.label: Ribosome composition
ced_current_atoms.statement: Ribosomes are composed of ribosomal RNA (rRNA) and protein.

ced_current_atoms.label: Ribosomes and common ancestry
ced_current_atoms.statement: Ribosomes are non-membrane subcellular structures found in cells in all forms of life and reflect common ancestry of all known life.

ced_current_atoms.label: Ribosome function
ced_current_atoms.statement: Ribosomes synthesize proteins according to messenger RNA (mRNA) sequences.

ced_current_atoms.label: Endomembrane system membership
ced_current_atoms.statement: The endomembrane system includes the endoplasmic reticulum, Golgi complex, lysosomes, vacuoles and transport vesicles, nuclear envelope, and plasma membrane.

ced_current_atoms.label: Endomembrane system function
ced_current_atoms.statement: Endomembrane-system components work together to modify, package, and transport polysaccharides, lipids, and proteins within and from cells.

ced_current_atoms.label: ER support and transport
ced_current_atoms.statement: The endoplasmic reticulum helps cells maintain shape and participates in intracellular transport.

ced_current_atoms.label: Rough ER
ced_current_atoms.statement: Rough ER is associated with membrane-bound ribosomes, contributes to compartmentalization, and helps carry out protein synthesis.

ced_current_atoms.label: Smooth ER
ced_current_atoms.statement: Smooth ER functions include cellular detoxification and lipid synthesis.

ced_current_atoms.label: Golgi structure
ced_current_atoms.statement: The Golgi complex is a membrane-bound structure consisting of a series of flattened membrane sacs.

ced_current_atoms.label: Golgi processing
ced_current_atoms.statement: Golgi functions include folding and chemically modifying newly synthesized cellular products.

ced_current_atoms.label: Golgi trafficking
ced_current_atoms.statement: Golgi functions include packaging proteins for trafficking.

ced_current_atoms.label: Mitochondrial double membrane
ced_current_atoms.statement: Mitochondria have a double membrane that creates compartments for different metabolic reactions involved in aerobic cellular respiration.

ced_current_atoms.label: Mitochondrial inner folds
ced_current_atoms.statement: The mitochondrial outer membrane is smooth and the inner membrane is highly folded; the folds increase membrane surface that supports efficient ATP synthesis.

ced_current_atoms.label: Lysosome digestion
ced_current_atoms.statement: Lysosomes are membrane-enclosed sacs containing hydrolytic enzymes that digest material.

ced_current_atoms.label: Lysosome apoptosis
ced_current_atoms.statement: Lysosomes also play a role in programmed cell death (apoptosis).

ced_current_atoms.label: Vacuole general
ced_current_atoms.statement: Vacuoles are membrane-bound sacs with diverse roles.

ced_current_atoms.label: Plant central vacuole
ced_current_atoms.statement: A specialized large plant-cell vacuole supports turgor pressure through nutrient and water storage.

ced_current_atoms.label: Animal vacuoles
ced_current_atoms.statement: Animal-cell vacuoles are smaller and more numerous than the large central vacuole typical of plant cells and can store cellular materials.

ced_current_atoms.label: Chloroplast distribution
ced_current_atoms.statement: Chloroplasts are specialized organelles found in plants and photosynthetic algae.

ced_current_atoms.label: Chloroplast structure/function
ced_current_atoms.statement: Chloroplasts have a double membrane and are the location of photosynthesis.

ced_current_atoms.label: SA:V exchange
ced_current_atoms.statement: Surface-area-to-volume ratio affects acquisition of nutrients, elimination of wastes, exchange of chemicals/energy, and acquisition or dissipation of thermal energy.

ced_current_atoms.label: Membrane area requirement
ced_current_atoms.statement: Plasma-membrane surface area must be sufficient to exchange materials for the volume it serves.

ced_current_atoms.label: Cell size limitation
ced_current_atoms.statement: Surface-area-to-volume ratio can restrict cell size and shape; smaller cells typically have a higher ratio and more efficient exchange with the environment than larger cells.

ced_current_atoms.label: Scaling with volume
ced_current_atoms.statement: As cell volume increases, surface-area-to-volume ratio decreases while internal resource demand increases.

ced_current_atoms.label: Exchange-surface adaptations
ced_current_atoms.statement: Membrane folds and other complex structures increase exchange surface area relative to volume.

ced_current_atoms.label: Body size and heat exchange
ced_current_atoms.statement: As organism size increases, surface-area-to-volume ratio and proportional heat exchange with the environment generally decrease.

ced_current_atoms.label: Body size and metabolic rate
ced_current_atoms.statement: Metabolic rate per unit body mass is generally higher in smaller multicellular organisms than in larger ones.

ced_current_atoms.label: Phospholipid amphipathic structure
ced_current_atoms.statement: Phospholipids have polar hydrophilic phosphate-containing regions and nonpolar hydrophobic fatty-acid regions.

ced_current_atoms.label: Bilayer orientation
ced_current_atoms.statement: Hydrophilic regions face aqueous internal/external environments while hydrophobic fatty-acid regions face one another in the membrane interior.

ced_current_atoms.label: Membrane-protein polarity
ced_current_atoms.statement: Embedded membrane proteins may contain hydrophilic regions, hydrophobic regions, or both.

ced_current_atoms.label: Protein orientation
ced_current_atoms.statement: Hydrophobic protein surfaces interact with the membrane interior; hydrophilic regions are exposed to aqueous environments or can occur within the protein interior.

ced_current_atoms.label: Fluid mosaic composition
ced_current_atoms.statement: Plasma membranes are phospholipid frameworks containing proteins, steroids such as cholesterol in vertebrate animals, glycoproteins, and glycolipids.

ced_current_atoms.label: Fluid mosaic movement
ced_current_atoms.statement: Many membrane lipids and proteins can move laterally within the membrane, producing the dynamic fluid-mosaic organization.

ced_current_atoms.label: Selective permeability basis
ced_current_atoms.statement: Plasma membranes separate internal and external environments; selective permeability results largely from the membrane hydrophobic interior.

ced_current_atoms.label: Small nonpolar passage
ced_current_atoms.statement: Small nonpolar molecules such as N2, O2, and CO2 can pass through the lipid bilayer readily.

ced_current_atoms.label: Hydrophilic transport
ced_current_atoms.statement: Large polar molecules and ions generally cross plasma membranes using embedded channels or transport proteins.

ced_current_atoms.label: Hydrophobic barrier
ced_current_atoms.statement: Nonpolar phospholipid tails impede direct passage of ions and many polar molecules.

ced_current_atoms.label: Small polar passage
ced_current_atoms.statement: Small uncharged polar molecules such as H2O and NH3 can pass through the membrane in small amounts.

ced_current_atoms.label: Cell walls
ced_current_atoms.statement: Cell walls of Bacteria, Archaea, Fungi, and plants provide structural boundaries and protection from osmotic lysis and can act as permeability barriers for some substances.

ced_current_atoms.label: Concentration gradients
ced_current_atoms.statement: Selective permeability permits concentration gradients of solutes to form across membranes.

ced_current_atoms.label: Passive transport
ced_current_atoms.statement: Passive transport is net movement from higher to lower concentration without direct input of metabolic energy.

ced_current_atoms.label: Active transport
ced_current_atoms.statement: Active transport requires direct energy input; in some cases it moves molecules from lower to higher concentration.

ced_current_atoms.label: Bulk transport energy
ced_current_atoms.statement: Endocytosis and exocytosis require energy to move large substances or large quantities of substances into and out of cells.

ced_current_atoms.label: Endocytosis
ced_current_atoms.statement: In endocytosis, the plasma membrane folds inward and forms vesicles that engulf material from the external environment.

ced_current_atoms.label: Exocytosis
ced_current_atoms.statement: In exocytosis, internal vesicles fuse with the plasma membrane and release material from the cell.

ced_current_atoms.label: Facilitated diffusion proteins
ced_current_atoms.statement: Facilitated diffusion uses channel or transport proteins to enable movement of substances that cannot readily cross the lipid bilayer.

ced_current_atoms.label: Ion channels
ced_current_atoms.statement: Charged ions such as Na+ and K+ require channel proteins to cross the membrane by facilitated diffusion.

ced_current_atoms.label: Membrane polarization
ced_current_atoms.statement: Ion movement across membranes can contribute to membrane polarization.

ced_current_atoms.label: Large polar facilitated diffusion
ced_current_atoms.statement: Large polar molecules can cross using facilitated diffusion without energy input when moving down their concentration gradient.

ced_current_atoms.label: Aquaporins
ced_current_atoms.statement: Aquaporins facilitate movement of large quantities of water across membranes.

ced_current_atoms.label: Tonicity relationships
ced_current_atoms.statement: An external solution may be hypotonic, hypertonic, or isotonic relative to a cell interior.

ced_current_atoms.label: Osmosis and water potential
ced_current_atoms.statement: Water moves by osmosis from regions of higher water potential to regions of lower water potential; this often corresponds to movement from hypotonic toward hypertonic regions.

ced_current_atoms.label: Water potential equation
ced_current_atoms.statement: Water potential is the sum of pressure potential and solute potential: Ψ = Ψp + Ψs.

ced_current_atoms.label: Membrane movement and homeostasis
ced_current_atoms.statement: Growth and homeostasis depend on continual movement of molecules across membranes.

ced_current_atoms.label: Osmoregulation
ced_current_atoms.statement: Osmoregulation maintains water balance and permits control of internal solute composition and water potential.

ced_current_atoms.label: Osmolarity direction
ced_current_atoms.statement: When other components are equal, water tends to move from lower osmolarity/solute concentration toward higher osmolarity/solute concentration.

ced_current_atoms.label: Solute potential equation
ced_current_atoms.statement: Solute potential can be calculated as Ψs = −iCRT, with i as ionization/van’t Hoff factor, C molar concentration, R pressure constant, and T Kelvin temperature.

ced_current_atoms.label: Energy for active transport
ced_current_atoms.statement: Metabolic energy such as ATP is required for active transport and for establishing/maintaining electrochemical gradients.

ced_current_atoms.label: Active transport proteins
ced_current_atoms.statement: Membrane proteins are necessary for active transport across membranes.

ced_current_atoms.label: Na+/K+ pump
ced_current_atoms.statement: The Na+/K+ pump is an ATPase that contributes to maintenance of membrane potential.

ced_current_atoms.label: Compartmentalization
ced_current_atoms.statement: Membranes and membrane-bound organelles compartmentalize intracellular metabolic processes and specific enzymatic reactions in eukaryotic cells.

ced_current_atoms.label: Minimizing competing interactions
ced_current_atoms.statement: Internal membranes facilitate cellular processes by separating reactions and minimizing competing interactions.

ced_current_atoms.label: Increasing reaction surface
ced_current_atoms.statement: Internal membranes increase surface area on which cellular reactions can occur.

ced_current_atoms.label: Endosymbiosis
ced_current_atoms.statement: Mitochondria and chloroplasts evolved from once free-living prokaryotic cells through endosymbiosis.

ced_current_atoms.label: Prokaryotic compartmentalization
ced_current_atoms.statement: Prokaryotes typically lack internal membrane-bound organelles but have internal regions with specialized structures and functions.

ced_current_atoms.label: Eukaryotic compartmentalization
ced_current_atoms.statement: Eukaryotic cells maintain internal membranes that partition the cell into specialized regions.

review_flags.source_claim: “Organelles: membrane bound structures in eukaryotes.”
review_flags.why_flagged: This treats membrane-boundedness as the universal definition of organelle, while the PPT itself later notes that ribosomes are sometimes classified differently.
review_flags.resolution: Use “membrane-bound organelles” for the relevant compartments; call ribosomes non-membrane subcellular structures as in the current CED.

review_flags.source_claim: “Unique Cell Components”: plants—chloroplasts, central vacuole, cell wall, plasmodesmata; animals—lysosomes, centrosomes, flagella.
review_flags.why_flagged: Several entries are not uniquely restricted to the listed kingdom; flagella occur in many eukaryotic lineages, centrosomes are not universal to animal cells, and plant lytic vacuoles perform lysosome-like functions.
review_flags.resolution: Teach these as common/characteristic examples in the course diagrams, not taxonomically unique universal traits.

review_flags.source_claim: Nuclear pores regulate entry/exit “from the cell”; DNA must leave the nucleus by first being transcribed; free-ribosome proteins function only in cytosol.
review_flags.why_flagged: The boundary is the nucleus, DNA generally remains nuclear, and free-ribosome products can be targeted to multiple non-endomembrane destinations.
review_flags.resolution: Canonical statements corrected using Campbell Ch.6; preserve source wording only in raw slide ledger.

review_flags.source_claim: “Peroxisomes: similar to lysosomes.”
review_flags.why_flagged: Peroxisomes and lysosomes are distinct organelles with different enzyme systems and primary functions.
review_flags.resolution: Teach peroxisomes as oxidative compartments; distinguish from lysosomal hydrolysis.

review_flags.source_claim: Mitochondria/chloroplasts are “capable of functioning on their own.”
review_flags.why_flagged: Modern mitochondria and chloroplasts are highly host-dependent and are not free-living cells.
review_flags.resolution: Use own DNA/ribosomes/division and bacterial similarities as evidence; explicitly reject modern independent-living claim.

review_flags.source_claim: Cristae “divide the mitochondria into two internal compartments.”
review_flags.why_flagged: The inner mitochondrial membrane separates matrix from intermembrane space; cristae are folds of that membrane that increase area.
review_flags.resolution: Canonical cristae statement corrected.

review_flags.source_claim: Matrix contains enzymes that “catalyze cellular respiration and produce ATP.”
review_flags.why_flagged: The matrix contains citric-acid-cycle and other enzymes, but most oxidative-phosphorylation ATP synthesis occurs via ATP synthase in the inner membrane.
review_flags.resolution: Separate matrix reactions from inner-membrane electron transport/ATP synthesis.

review_flags.source_claim: “Light dependent reactions occur in grana.”
review_flags.why_flagged: Light reactions occur in thylakoid membranes; grana are stacks of thylakoids.
review_flags.resolution: Use thylakoid membrane as the reaction location; grana remains structural vocabulary.

review_flags.source_claim: Microtubules grow from the centrosome.
review_flags.why_flagged: Centrosomes are major microtubule-organizing centers in many animal cells, but not a universal eukaryotic rule.
review_flags.resolution: Qualify to animal cells/microtubule-organizing centers.

review_flags.source_claim: Intermediate filaments are “permanent structural elements.”
review_flags.why_flagged: Intermediate filaments are comparatively stable but still dynamic and remodelable.
review_flags.resolution: Use “relatively stable structural elements.”

review_flags.source_claim: Integral proteins are “aka transmembrane proteins.”
review_flags.why_flagged: Transmembrane proteins are a subset of integral proteins; some integral proteins do not span the entire bilayer.
review_flags.resolution: Distinguish integral from transmembrane.

review_flags.source_claim: Plant cell wall provides “regulation of water intake.”
review_flags.why_flagged: The wall mechanically resists expansion and contributes to water relations, while selective membrane transport is governed primarily by the plasma membrane.
review_flags.resolution: Canonical cell-wall function corrected.

review_flags.source_claim: Osmosis described as water moving from low solute to high solute, and water-potential slide lists separate low-solute/high-solute and high-pressure/low-pressure rules.
review_flags.why_flagged: These are useful under restricted conditions, but net water movement is governed by total water potential when both solute and pressure differ.
review_flags.resolution: Use Ψ high→low as the governing rule; low-solute→high-solute only when other water-potential components are equal.

review_flags.source_claim: Unequal ion concentrations “result in an electrical charge.”
review_flags.why_flagged: Membrane potential is a voltage from charge separation across a membrane; bulk solutions remain nearly electrically neutral.
review_flags.resolution: Canonical membrane-potential statement corrected.

review_flags.source_claim: ATP transfers a terminal phosphate to “the transport protein” as the general active-transport mechanism.
review_flags.why_flagged: Direct phosphorylation occurs in some pumps, including P-type ATPases, but is not universal to all active transport.
review_flags.resolution: Use this mechanism for the Na+/K+ ATPase example, not as the definition of all active transport.

review_flags.source_claim: Endocytosis described as uptake “from vesicles fused from the plasma membrane”; pinocytosis defined as uptake in a protein-coated vesicle.
review_flags.why_flagged: Endocytic vesicles form by membrane invagination/pinching off; pinocytosis is not defined by a single coating mechanism.
review_flags.resolution: Canonical bulk-transport statements corrected.

review_flags.source_claim: Hypertonic conditions cause cells to “shrivel and die.”
review_flags.why_flagged: Cells lose water and shrink; death depends on severity, duration, and cell type.
review_flags.resolution: Teach shrinkage/plasmolysis as direct effects; do not make death inevitable.

review_flags.source_claim: Packet uses legacy AP codes SYI-1.D through EVO-1.B and eleven topic numbers.
review_flags.why_flagged: The current Fall 2025 CED uses Unit 2 Topics 2.1–2.10 with revised learning-objective/essential-knowledge codes and some scope redistribution.
review_flags.resolution: Preserve legacy packet codes as historical teacher-source metadata; map all canonical records to current 2025 CED topics/codes.

review_flags.source_claim: Cytoskeleton, centrosome, actin, intermediate filaments, detailed chloroplast/mitochondrial subcompartments and several transport subtypes receive extensive teacher coverage.
review_flags.why_flagged: Much of this detail is not explicitly required in the current 2025 CED Unit 2 essential knowledge.
review_flags.resolution: Keep as TEACHER_REQUIRED_ENRICHMENT where classroom responsibility is clear; do not label it AP-required solely because it appears in teacher materials.

review_flags.source_claim: “Remember: all formulas are given to you on the AP exam.”
review_flags.why_flagged: The current CED lists relevant equations, but a blanket promise that every formula will always be supplied should not become a scientific/curricular memory target.
review_flags.resolution: Retain formulas and calculation fluency; omit the blanket guarantee from canonical student science.

Eukaryotic cells have DNA enclosed in a nucleus and contain membrane-bound organelles.

Nuclear pore complexes regulate movement of macromolecules between the nucleus and cytoplasm.
The nucleolus is a nuclear region where rRNA is transcribed and ribosomal subunits are assembled with imported proteins before export through nuclear pores.

Free ribosomes synthesize proteins that mainly function in the cytosol, while some free-ribosome products are targeted after translation to organelles such as the nucleus, mitochondria, chloroplasts, and peroxisomes.
Ribosomes bound to rough ER or the nuclear envelope generally synthesize proteins destined for secretion, membranes, or compartments of the endomembrane system.
The ER is a network of membranous tubules and sacs called cisternae; its membrane separates the ER lumen from the cytosol.
Depending on cell type, smooth ER can participate in carbohydrate metabolism, detoxification, calcium storage, and lipid synthesis.
The cis face of the Golgi receives vesicles arriving from the ER.
The trans face of the Golgi sorts and dispatches vesicles toward cellular destinations or the plasma membrane.
Golgi cisternae are distinct flattened membranous sacs arranged in stacks.
During autophagy, damaged cellular material is enclosed and delivered to lysosomes for enzymatic breakdown and recycling.

Chlorophyll pigments in thylakoid membranes absorb light used in photosynthesis.
The cytoskeleton is a dynamic network of protein fibers that supports cell shape, organizes cell contents, and contributes to intracellular and whole-cell movement.
Microtubules are hollow tubulin polymers that help maintain cell shape, serve as tracks for motor proteins, form the mitotic spindle, and form the core of eukaryotic cilia and flagella.
In many animal cells, microtubules are nucleated from a centrosome; other eukaryotic cells use other microtubule-organizing centers.
Microfilaments are thin actin filaments that bear tension, support cell shape, participate in cell motility and muscle contraction, and form the contractile ring during animal-cell cytokinesis.

Intermediate filaments are rope-like cytoskeletal elements that reinforce cell shape, anchor organelles, and form structures such as the nuclear lamina; they are relatively stable compared with many microtubules and actin filaments.

canonical_catalog.canonical_label: Surface area and volume of sphere
canonical_catalog.canonical_verified_statement: For a sphere, surface area is 4πr² and volume is 4/3πr³; therefore SA:V decreases as radius increases.
Unsaturated phospholipid tails contain cis double-bond kinks that reduce tight packing and help membranes remain fluid at lower temperatures.

In vertebrate animal membranes, cholesterol restrains phospholipid movement at higher temperatures and hinders tight packing at lower temperatures, buffering membrane fluidity across temperature changes.
Integral membrane proteins penetrate the hydrophobic interior of the bilayer; some, but not all, span the entire membrane as transmembrane proteins.
Peripheral membrane proteins are loosely associated with the membrane surface or with exposed parts of integral proteins and do not penetrate the bilayer hydrophobic core.
A glycolipid is a membrane lipid with a covalently attached carbohydrate that can participate in cell recognition and interactions.
A glycoprotein is a membrane protein with a covalently attached carbohydrate; membrane carbohydrates are important in cell-cell recognition.
Primary plant cell walls contain cellulose microfibrils embedded in a matrix of other polysaccharides and proteins.
The plant cell wall supports shape, resists excessive expansion during water uptake, and protects the cell; selective transport into the cytoplasm is controlled primarily by the plasma membrane.
Plasmodesmata are membrane-lined channels through plant cell walls that connect the cytoplasm of adjacent cells and support intercellular transport and communication.
Diffusion is net movement resulting from random molecular motion, with net movement down a concentration gradient until dynamic equilibrium is approached.
Osmosis is net diffusion of free water across a selectively permeable membrane from higher water potential toward lower water potential.
Channel proteins provide hydrophilic passageways for specific ions or molecules; many are gated by chemical or physical stimuli.
Carrier proteins bind specific solutes and change conformation to move them across the membrane.
Membrane potential is the voltage across a membrane created by separation of charge associated with unequal ion distributions across the membrane.
An electrogenic pump generates voltage across a membrane by moving net charge and can create electrochemical gradients used by other cellular processes.
For each ATP hydrolyzed, the animal-cell Na+/K+ ATPase exports 3 Na+ and imports 2 K+, producing a net outward movement of one positive charge and maintaining ion gradients.
Proton pumps use energy to move H+ across membranes and establish electrochemical proton gradients.
Cotransport couples downhill movement of one solute to uphill movement of another by using energy stored in an electrochemical gradient.
Plant cells can import sucrose against its concentration gradient by coupling sucrose uptake to H+ moving down a proton electrochemical gradient through a symporter.
Phagocytosis is a form of endocytosis in which a cell engulfs large particles; in many animal cells the resulting vesicle can fuse with a lysosome for digestion.
Pinocytosis is nonspecific uptake of extracellular fluid and dissolved solutes into small vesicles; it can occur through several molecular mechanisms and is not defined by a single protein coat.
Receptor-mediated endocytosis concentrates specific extracellular ligands after they bind membrane receptors, followed by membrane invagination and vesicle formation.
Tonicity describes how a solution containing nonpenetrating solutes causes a cell to gain or lose water.
In an isotonic environment, there is no net water movement across the membrane, although water continues moving in both directions.
A cell in a hypertonic environment loses water; animal cells shrink and plant cells may plasmolyze. Water loss does not necessarily mean immediate cell death.
A cell in a hypotonic environment gains water; animal cells can swell and lyse, while a healthy plant cell becomes turgid as the cell wall resists expansion.
Plasmolysis occurs when a plant cell loses water and the plasma membrane pulls away from the cell wall.
Turgor pressure is the pressure generated as water enters a plant cell and the cell contents press against the cell wall; it helps support nonwoody plant tissues.
Pressure potential is the physical pressure component of water potential; in an open beaker at atmospheric pressure it is conventionally treated as zero relative pressure.
Adding dissolved solute lowers solute potential; solute potential is zero for pure water under the standard convention and is negative for solutions.
Mitochondria and chloroplasts contain their own circular DNA, supporting descent from bacterial endosymbionts.
Mitochondria and chloroplasts replicate by division processes similar to bacterial binary fission.
Mitochondrial and chloroplast ribosomes have features more similar to bacterial ribosomes than to eukaryotic cytosolic ribosomes.
Mitochondria and chloroplasts have double membranes and inner-membrane systems with bacterial similarities consistent with endosymbiotic origins.
Modern mitochondria and chloroplasts are not generally capable of independent free-living existence; many genes and functions are integrated with the host cell.
